p01-ctx-t.name: p01-ctx-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p01-ctx-t.text: **Used on this page**: design matrix $X$ (one row per sample), target vector $\mathbf{y}$, weights $\mathbf{w}$; residual $\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{y}-X\mathbf{w}$.

p01-c2-t.text:
Learning goals: organize the design matrix and target vector; derive the normal equation and explain the pseudoinverse; check Example 3.4
In one line: least squares minimizes the sum of squared errors on the data in hand, not the number of classification mistakes
A tailor fits all sizes with one fixed rule; small size error does not mean every label is right

p02-title.name: p02-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p02-title.text: Design matrix: one row per sample; squared errors form a length

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p02-bridge.name: p02-bridge

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p02-bridge.text: Last page: solve in one batch. This page puts each sample in a matrix row and writes the sum of squares.

p02-ctx-t.name: p02-ctx-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p02-ctx-t.text: **Used on this page**: $N$ samples, $d$ features after augmenting; row $i$ of $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}$ is $\mathbf{a}_i^T$; $J(\mathbf{w})=\|\mathbf{y}-X\mathbf{w}\|^2$.

p02-fig-title.name: p02-fig-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p02-fig-title.text: Data $\rightarrow$ matrix $\rightarrow$ prediction $\rightarrow$ residual $\rightarrow$ sum of squares

p02-c2-t.name: p02-c2-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p02-c2-t.text:
$J(\mathbf{w})=\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mathbf{a}_i^T\mathbf{w})^2=\|\mathbf{y}-X\mathbf{w}\|^2$; divide by the fixed $N$ for the empirical MSE, with the same minimizing weights
Population MSE takes an expectation over the distribution, LS sums over finite data; with unknown distribution, samples estimate the population moments
So do not say MSE needs the full distribution

p02-ban-t.name: p02-ban-t

p02-ban-t.text: Takeaway: least squares adds up all squared residuals of the finite data and minimizes them.

p03-title.text: Normal equation $X^{T}Xw = X^{T}y$: residual perpendicular to columns

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-bridge.name: p03-bridge

p03-ctx-t.name: p03-ctx-t

p03-ctx-t.text: **Used on this page**: $J=\mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{y}-2\mathbf{w}^TX^T\mathbf{y}+\mathbf{w}^TX^TX\mathbf{w}$; with full column rank, $X^TX$ is invertible.

p03-fig-title.name: p03-fig-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-c2-t.text:
The gradient's minus sign comes from differentiating $\mathbf{y}-X\mathbf{w}$ with respect to the weights
$X^T\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{0}$: the residual is perpendicular to every column of $X$, exactly the projection geometry from two units ago
When the columns are linearly independent (full column rank), $X^TX$ is invertible and the weights are unique

steps.label: Goal: solve least squares in one… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Goal: solve least squares in one… · 1/3 · Female: Last unit's LMS corrects one sample at a time. If all the data are already in, must we still go one by one? Think: is there a more direct way?

narration.label: s1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Last unit's LMS corrects one sample at a time. If all the data are already in, must we still go one by one? Think: is there a more direct way?

steps.label: Goal: solve least squares in one… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Goal: solve least squares in one… · 2/3 · Male: Yes. This unit has three goals: arrange finite data into a design matrix and a target vector; derive the normal equation and say when the pseudoinverse applies; and finally check Example 3.4's weights, residual and classification errors.

narration.label: s2.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Yes. This unit has three goals: arrange finite data into a design matrix and a target vector; derive the normal equation and say when the pseudoinverse applies; and finally check Example 3.4's weights, residual and classification errors.

steps.label: Goal: solve least squares in one… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Goal: solve least squares in one… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: once the data are in, write all errors as one objective and solve directly. Note least squares minimizes the sum of squared errors, not the number of classification mistakes.

narration.label: s3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: once the data are in, write all errors as one objective and solve directly. Note least squares minimizes the sum of squared errors, not the number of classification mistakes.

steps.label: Design matrix: one row per… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Design matrix: one row per… · 1/3 · Male: First, organize the data. Each augmented sample becomes one row of the matrix, so the design matrix has N rows, each ending in the constant 1. The matrix times the weights gives all predictions, and target minus prediction gives the residual vector. Think: what is the sum of squared errors?

narration.label: s4.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: First, organize the data. Each augmented sample becomes one row of the matrix, so the design matrix has N rows, each ending in the constant 1. The matrix times the weights gives all predictions, and target minus prediction gives the residual vector. Think: what is the sum of squared errors?

steps.label: Design matrix: one row per… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Design matrix: one row per… · 2/3 · Female: It is the squared length of the residual vector. Divide by the fixed N for the empirical mean squared error; the minimizing weights are the same. Population MSE takes an expectation over the distribution, LS sums over finite data, and samples can estimate it when the distribution is unknown.

narration.label: s5.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: It is the squared length of the residual vector. Divide by the fixed N for the empirical mean squared error; the minimizing weights are the same. Population MSE takes an expectation over the distribution, LS sums over finite data, and samples can estimate it when the distribution is unknown.

steps.label: Design matrix: one row per… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Design matrix: one row per… · 3/3 · Male: Take this away: least squares adds up all squared residuals of the finite data and minimizes them. Next page, set the gradient to zero.

narration.label: s6.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: Take this away: least squares adds up all squared residuals of the finite data and minimizes them. Next page, set the gradient to zero.

steps.label: Normal equation X^{T}Xw = X^{T}y… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Normal equation X^{T}Xw = X^{T}y… · 1/3 · Female: Expand the square and differentiate. The gradient is minus 2 times X transpose times the residual, and the minus sign comes from differentiating the residual with respect to the weights. Set it to zero and the residual is perpendicular to every column of X. Think: how does this relate to projection?

narration.label: s7.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Expand the square and differentiate. The gradient is minus 2 times X transpose times the residual, and the minus sign comes from differentiating the residual with respect to the weights. Set it to zero and the residual is perpendicular to every column of X. Think: how does this relate to projection?

steps.label: Normal equation X^{T}Xw = X^{T}y… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Normal equation X^{T}Xw = X^{T}y… · 2/3 · Male: It is projection. The normal equation is X transpose X times w equals X transpose y. If the columns are linearly independent, meaning full column rank, X transpose X is invertible, and the weights are unique, written as the pseudoinverse times y.

narration.label: s8.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: It is projection. The normal equation is X transpose X times w equals X transpose y. If the columns are linearly independent, meaning full column rank, X transpose X is invertible, and the weights are unique, written as the pseudoinverse times y.

steps.label: Normal equation X^{T}Xw = X^{T}y… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Normal equation X^{T}Xw = X^{T}y… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: the least-squares solution makes the residual perpendicular to every column of the design matrix. Next page, what happens if columns repeat?

narration.label: s9.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Take this away: the least-squares solution makes the residual perpendicular to every column of the design matrix. Next page, what happens if columns repeat?

steps.label: Pseudoinverse: repeated columns… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Pseudoinverse: repeated columns… · 1/3 · Male: In this example, the two columns of X are identical, so X transpose X is not invertible. In the figure, every point on the green line, where w1 plus w2 equals 1, fits exactly. Guess: which point does the pseudoinverse pick?

narration.label: s10.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: In this example, the two columns of X are identical, so X transpose X is not invertible. In the figure, every point on the green line, where w1 plus w2 equals 1, fits exactly. Guess: which point does the pseudoinverse pick?

steps.label: Pseudoinverse: repeated columns… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Pseudoinverse: repeated columns… · 2/3 · Female: The one nearest the origin, 0.5, 0.5, with squared weight length 0.5, smaller than 1 for 1, 0. Note the inverse of X transpose X times X transpose applies only with full column rank; in general use the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. The projected prediction stays unique.

narration.label: s11.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The one nearest the origin, 0.5, 0.5, with squared weight length 0.5, smaller than 1 for 1, 0. Note the inverse of X transpose X times X transpose applies only with full column rank; in general use the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. The projected prediction stays unique.

steps.label: Pseudoinverse: repeated columns… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Pseudoinverse: repeated columns… · 3/3 · Male: Take this away: among many least-squares solutions, the pseudoinverse picks the shortest one. Next page, Example 3.4's ten points.

narration.label: s12.mp3

steps.speakerNotes: Solving: clear to integer… · 2/3 · Female: Integer coefficients are easier to check. Eliminating the bias leaves two equations with determinant 49720. The weights are minus 4000 over 1243 and 300 over 1243, and the bias is 1779 over 1243.

steps.label: Added check: the midpoint, not an… · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes: Added check: the midpoint, not an… · 1/3 · Female: A common misreading: this least-squares line misclassifies, so the data must be nonseparable. That inference fails. In the figure, the midpoint of the line joining the two blue positives is exactly the orange negative point. Think: what does that mean?

narration.label: s19.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: A common misreading: this least-squares line misclassifies, so the data must be nonseparable. That inference fails. In the figure, the midpoint of the line joining the two blue positives is exactly the orange negative point. Think: what does that mean?

steps.label: Added check: the midpoint, not an… · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Added check: the midpoint, not an… · 2/3 · Male: A linear score is affine. If both endpoints score positive, the midpoint scores their average, which is also positive. But the negative point needs a negative score, a contradiction, so no line can get them all right.

narration.label: s20.mp3
narration.transcript: Male: A linear score is affine. If both endpoints score positive, the midpoint scores their average, which is also positive. But the negative point needs a negative score, a contradiction, so no line can get them all right.

steps.label: Added check: the midpoint, not an… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Added check: the midpoint, not an… · 3/3 · Female: Take this away: the negative point is the midpoint of two positives, so no single line can get all of them right. One LS line misclassifying is not evidence in itself.

narration.label: s21.mp3

steps.label: Myth: the smallest squared error… · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Myth: the smallest squared error… · 3/3 · Male: Take this away: least squares is the best numerical fit, not the fewest classification errors. Forming X transpose X squares the condition number, so in practice do not form an explicit inverse. Next page, your turn.
